docs.title: Large Language Models & Agent Tools
docs.text: This is the first page of the roadmap on purpose. Not because these tools are exciting, but because they change what everything after them costs you. A question that used to mean a week of fighting with someone else's code can now be a conversation, and the bottleneck moves from "can I write the code" to "do I understand the problem." So this page is a map: a quick look at the language model underneath, why the tools are worth your time, what the confusingly similar ones actually are, how to start, and how to use them to amplify what you can do.

docs.title: The model underneath
docs.text:
The engine inside every coding agent is a large language model (LLM), and it earns a few paragraphs up front. What it has learned to do is almost disappointingly simple: after reading an enormous amount of text, given everything so far, guess which word comes next. The fluent answers in a chat window are what that guessing game looks like after a trillion rounds of practice. Keep this in mind and a lot of later strangeness makes sense. The model is not a database, so nothing it says is guaranteed true, and it has no lasting memory beyond the context window you show it, a term that will keep coming up on this page. When an agent confidently states something false, or seems to become a different person late in a long session, the root cause is one of those two facts.

The way people use these models has changed shape a few times. First came the chatbot era, one question for one answer, where the skill worth studying was writing a good prompt; prompt engineering is a word from that period. Then models learned to think before answering, and reasoning models turned "work through it step by step" from a prompt trick into a built-in habit, so careful phrasing mattered less. The most recent change put the model in a loop with tools, letting it read files, run commands, look at what came back, and decide what to do next. That is an agent. The human skill moved with it: away from crafting the perfect sentence, toward setting up a good environment with a clear goal, capable tools, and a way for the agent to check its own work. The "delegate, don't dictate" advice later on this page is the everyday version of that shift.

If you want these foundations in one sitting, set aside half an hour for LLM Fundamentals. It runs interactively in the browser with nothing to install, and it covers the layer underneath everything above: what a system prompt really does, why the model thinks in numbers rather than words, why overstuffing the context window backfires, and why too many tools slow a model down. A short list of concepts, but each one will come up daily.

docs.title: Why this comes first
docs.text:
A coding agent is a program that takes a goal in plain language, then reads files, runs commands, and edits code on its own until the goal is met or it gets stuck. Paired with the command line and git, it turns the terminal from a wall into something you can talk to.

This matters whether you do experiments or write code, for two reasons. First, a coding agent runs anywhere, not only in a folder full of code. Anthropic's docs point out it works as well in a folder of notes or manuscripts as in a repository, and this site, including the page you are reading, was written that way. There is a walk-through in Writing This Site With Claude Code. Second, the barrier really does seem to be understanding rather than coding. Across roughly 400,000 sessions, Anthropic found that domain expertise, not coding skill, was what separated people who got useful results from people who did not. That number comes from the company selling the tool and rests on a metric they designed, so take it with a grain of salt. The independent version of the same signal: in January 2026, MIT dedicated a session of Missing Semester to agentic coding. A university opening a course on a topic says plenty about how much it matters.

For this lab, these tools are already a must-learn. Claude Science, out in mid-2026, ships tools for genomics, single-cell, and structural biology, and it drives jobs on an HPC cluster over SSH, submitting them with sbatch instead of running them on the login node. Edison Scientific's Kosmos takes another path, positioning itself as an "AI scientist" that reads the literature, analyzes data, and generates hypotheses on its own for biopharma R&D. Whether or not you use these products, expect tools like them to become more and more common.

docs.title: Three tools that look alike
docs.text:
The most useful thing to sort out early: "chatbot," "coding agent," and things like OpenClaw and Hermes look like three products of the same kind. They are not. They are the same model wearing three different amounts of clothing. The model is identical, and in every case it runs in a datacenter rather than on your laptop. What changes is the harness around it, meaning the tools it can call and the things it is allowed to touch.

flowchart TB
    C1["<b>Web chatbot</b><br/><i>sees only what you paste in</i>"] --- M
    C2["<b>Coding agent</b><br/><i>your files, your shell, your git</i>"] --- M
    C3["<b>Agent assistant</b><br/><i>your whole machine and your accounts</i>"] --- M
    M["<b>The same model</b> · running in a datacenter, not on your laptop"]

Figure: one model, three harnesses. Left to right, the harness reaches more of your world, which is the same axis as both the usefulness and the risk.

Web chatbot Coding agent Agent assistant For example claude.ai, ChatGPT Claude Code, Codex CLI, Kimi Code, Z Code OpenClaw, Hermes Where the harness runs vendor's server, in a browser tab your machine, a terminal or editor your machine, in the background What it can reach only what you paste in your working folder, shell, and git your whole machine and your accounts Does it loop? no, one reply per message yes, runs tools until the job is done yes, and can start a turn on its own Can you undo it? nothing to undo yes, through git not by default

The taxonomy earns its keep because those same properties predict both the power and the danger. A chatbot cannot delete your files because it cannot see them. A coding agent can, which is exactly why running it inside git matters: every change it makes is a diff you can read and revert. Agent assistants like OpenClaw and Hermes go further, wiring the model into your mail, chat, and calendar so they can act without you starting each turn. That is where things are heading, but tools in this category are still immature: get to know them gradually, and use them with care.

For the concepts underneath all this, Simon Willison's one-line definition of an agent ("an LLM agent runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal") and Anthropic's Building Effective Agents are the two clearest short reads. In Chinese, the video 一口气拆穿 Skill/MCP/RAG/Agent 底层逻辑 does the same in fifteen minutes, and it aims straight at the real problem, which is that everyone uses these words and nobody defines them.

docs.title: Getting your hands on one
docs.text:
Getting started is simple: open a terminal and install one. Anthropic's setup guide walks you through it, the Quickstart takes you from install to a first real edit, and the terminal guide is there for anyone who has never used a command line.

Claude Code is not the only choice. Tools like Kimi Code and Zhipu's Z Code work much the same way; Kimi Code installs with a single command (curl -fsSL https://code.kimi.com/kimi-code/install.sh | bash) and starts with kimi. The concepts and habits on this page transfer across all of them, so picking one and getting good at it matters more than picking the perfect one.

The terminal is still worth learning properly, because git and the cluster live there, and it is the line between watching the agent work and being able to check it. If you want to go deeper, Linux, Git & GitHub Basics covers the shell and version control, and Python Basics covers the language most of the lab's analysis is written in.

One practical note: the capable coding agents are paid, but the money is well spent, and the lab fully supports members spending on these tools.

docs.title: Talking to it well
docs.text:
Most people arrive from chatbots with the instinct to write one careful, detailed instruction and hope. With an agent that is close to backwards, and two habits matter more than any amount of prompt phrasing.

The first is to delegate rather than dictate. Hand it the whole project and a goal and let it open files, search, and try things, instead of pasting snippets into a box and describing what you want done to them. It was trained on exactly the kind of poking-around the terminal allows, and it does far more when you let it look than when you narrate.

The second is to give it something it can check itself against. An agent stops when the work looks done, so a test to run or a build to pass keeps it going until the check is green, rather than leaving you to be the error message. That single habit buys more reliability than any wording trick.

For the details, three resources are enough. Anthropic's prompting best practices is the canonical reference and shorter than you would guess. The Claude Code best practices post has before-and-after examples and one trick worth stealing: ask the agent to interview you about a task and write the spec down before it starts. If you would rather learn the mindset than the syntax, Anthropic Academy's free AI Fluency course is built around delegation and judgment instead of prompt recipes. Anything, in any language, that sells a list of magic phrases is safe to skip; on current models that material is mostly obsolete.

docs.title: The words you'll keep hearing
docs.text:
A small vocabulary comes up over and over. None of it needs to be understood deeply to start, and trying to master it first is a good way to stall. One line each, and where to go when a word starts getting in your way.

Concept What it is Start here Model & effort Which model runs, and how hard it works before answering. Reach for a bigger model when it understood the task and still got it wrong; raise effort when it was careless. Choosing a model and effort Context window Everything the model can see at once. It fills up over a long session, and quality drops when it does. Explore the context window Skills A folder that teaches an agent a procedure, loaded only when it is needed. Now a shared standard several tools read. agentskills.io MCP One common plug for connecting an agent to outside systems like a database. Now stewarded by the Linux Foundation, not Anthropic. modelcontextprotocol.io Subagents A helper that does a noisy side job in its own context and reports back a summary, so the main thread stays clean. Claude Code docs

The lab keeps its own Skills, packaged as a Claude Code plugin, over on Routine Lab Support. Once you are comfortable, that is where the tools stop being generic and start knowing about our data.

docs.title: Learning it systematically
docs.text:
If you want to learn it systematically through a course, the one to take is DeepLearning.AI's short course Claude Code: A Highly Agentic Coding Assistant, built with Anthropic and taught by its head of technical education. It runs from CLAUDE.md and context management all the way to subagents, hooks, and MCP, with three full project exercises along the way; some Python and git helps. The full videos are also mirrored on Bilibili.

The course uses Claude Code, but what you learn is not locked to it: context management, subagents, hooks, and MCP mean the same thing in the other coding agents, so everything transfers when you switch to Kimi Code, Z Code, or whatever comes next.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Building Effective Agents: the best short case for keeping agent setups simple, and it reads well once the vocabulary above has stopped being a fog.
  • learn.shareai.run: a natively Chinese course on why Claude Code behaves the way it does. Deep, close to a source-code-level dissection of Claude, for when you want the principles.
  • MIT's Missing Semester, the January 2026 session: dedicated to agentic coding, and a good way to walk the whole toolchain end to end.

docs.title: Linux, Git & GitHub Basics
docs.text: The command line, git, and GitHub are the foundation of the lab's daily workflow: typed commands drive the computing on our servers, git records every change, and GitHub shares that history with other people. Sharpening these tools pays for itself; together with Python they are what all our computing and analysis runs on, and Python gets its own page in Python Basics. These three are also the skills a coding agent leans on hardest, so the point of learning them has shifted: not memorizing commands, but reading what the agent did and judging whether it was necessary. This page picks out the basics worth learning, a few entry-level resources, and a few places to check whether the material actually stuck.

docs.title: Why the terminal is still worth learning
docs.text:
The reasons are practical. First, most of the lab's computing does not happen on your laptop: sequencing data is too big and alignment too slow, so the work runs on servers and clusters that have no desktop and no mouse, and what greets you after you log in over SSH is a shell. Second, most bioinformatics tools have no graphical interface at all, so using them means typing commands. Third, typing is where the efficiency comes from: the shell's idea is to chain small single-purpose tools with pipes, each one's output feeding the next, so "count how often each sequence occurs across a pile of FASTQ files and list the top ten" is one line of grep, sort and uniq, while opening those files in an editor stops being possible once they reach tens of gigabytes. Commands saved in a script can also be rerun anytime and handed to someone else exactly as they were.

Two words people mix up constantly: the terminal is the window on your screen, and the shell is the program inside it that reads what you type and runs it, usually bash or zsh. Linux is the operating system nearly all of these machines run, which is why "learning Linux" and "learning the command line" are, for our purposes, the same thing.

The arrival of coding agents has made all this more central, not less. Agents were trained on exactly this world of terminals and text streams, so the command line is where they are strongest, as the previous page describes. What becomes scarce is the ability to read commands rather than type them: knowing what rm -rf does before letting it run, and being able to tell whether the agent's one-liner answers the question you asked or some other question.

docs.title: Learning the shell
docs.text:
The order that works, in our experience, is files first, streams second, remote machines third. Start with moving around and looking at things: ls, cd, cat, less, mkdir, cp, mv, rm. Then learn to think in streams: pipes, redirection, grep, wc, and a loop for the moment you catch yourself running the same command ten times. Only then go remote with ssh and scp, which is also when the cluster stops being an abstraction. That much is honestly enough for daily lab work; a script, meaning a string of commands saved in a file for the shell to run from top to bottom, will suggest itself once you are tired of retyping.

For a first course we like Data Carpentry's shell-genomics: it teaches exactly these skills inside a genomics project, on real FASTQ files from an E. coli variant-calling dataset, so every command comes with a reason to care. It does expect the workshop's cloud setup, which takes some work to recreate on your own; if you'd rather start with zero preparation on your own laptop, pick Software Carpentry's shell-novice, which runs locally with a small download and takes an afternoon. Either way, keep 阮一峰's Bash 脚本教程 open on the side as the Chinese reference you look things up in. If lectures suit you better than guided workshops, MIT's Missing Semester compresses the same ground into a few dense sessions, good for a fast review pass once you have finished one of the courses. That is the whole reading list; depth can wait until a real problem asks for it.

Knowing whether it stuck is its own step, and three free sites check you at increasing levels of realism. Linux Survival ends each short module with a quiz that asks you to type the right command, good for a ten-minute recall check. cmdchallenge gives you one puzzle per command in a browser terminal and verifies your answer automatically, no account needed. OverTheWire's Bandit is the capstone: you log into a real server over SSH and each level's password unlocks the next, so progress is proof. Levels 0 to 15 cover the basics on this page, and being able to do them without looking things up is a solid working definition of "I know the command line."

One more suggestion, the fun kind. Hacknet is a story-driven hacking game, cheap on Steam and officially localized into Simplified Chinese, played entirely by typing into a terminal. Its everyday commands are real Unix, ls, cd, cat, rm, ps, kill, and the campaign doubles as a tutorial that introduces them one at a time. The hacking itself is simplified fantasy and there are no pipes or permissions, so what it teaches is comfort with the terminal rather than security skills. As a way to stop being afraid of the black window, it works surprisingly well.

docs.title: Git, the lab notebook for code
docs.text:
Git is a version control system: it records the history of a folder as a series of commits, each one a snapshot with a message explaining why it exists. Once a project is in git, "I broke something and I don't know when" stops being scary, because every earlier state is one command away. Branches let you try an idea in a parallel draft without touching the working version. And for working with a coding agent, git is what makes delegation safe: every change the agent makes is a diff you can read and revert, which is exactly why the previous page insists on running agents inside git.

The mental model worth building early is that your code exists in four places at once:

flowchart LR
    A["<b>Working folder</b><br/><i>the files you edit</i>"] -- "git add" --> B["<b>Staging area</b><br/><i>the next snapshot being assembled</i>"]
    B -- "git commit" --> C["<b>Local repository</b><br/><i>the full history on your machine</i>"]
    C -- "git push" --> D["<b>Remote</b><br/><i>GitHub or Gitee</i>"]
    D -- "git pull" --> C

Figure: the four places a change passes through. Most confusion with git is confusion about which of these you are looking at.

For learning, two resources cover the basics. 廖雪峰的 Git 教程 is the standard Chinese first read: zero assumed background, command by command with screenshots, deliberately limited to the commands you actually need. Then Learn Git Branching, an interactive sandbox with an animated commit tree and a full Chinese interface. Branching and merging are where tutorials stop helping and intuition has to grow, and nothing grows it faster.

Learn Git Branching doubles as the self-check: each level shows a target commit tree and only passes when yours matches the goal, so finishing the main and remote tracks means the skill is really there. To prove it transfers to the real thing, gitexercises.fracz.com gives you a local repository and grades your work server-side each time you run git verify. Those two passing you is a better signal than any amount of rereading.

docs.title: GitHub, and Gitee
docs.text:
GitHub is where the remote in that diagram usually lives, but it earns its place for a different reason: it is where open science happens. Nearly every tool and dataset this roadmap mentions lives there as a public repository with its code, its issues, and its discussions attached, and reading a tool's repository is a research skill in itself. The two constructs to learn are the pull request, a proposal to merge your changes into another history with room for review, and the issue, a tracked thread for a bug or a plan.

If you don't have accounts yet, go register on GitHub and Gitee first; the exercises below all happen in your own account. The fastest way in is GitHub's own Hello World, a ten-minute exercise done entirely in the browser, no installation, that walks through repository, branch, commit, and pull request. Then let GitHub Skills check you: its free courses run inside your own account and a bot reviews each step of your work automatically, so finishing the Introduction to GitHub course is itself the proof you can handle the workflow.

From mainland China, GitHub is reachable but often slow, and Gitee, run by OSChina, is the domestic alternative worth knowing. It speaks exactly the same git, so clone, push, branches, and pull requests all work as you would expect, and a repository can have both as remotes: push to GitHub for the world, and to Gitee for fast access at home. The honest caveats: publishing a public repository on Gitee requires passing a content review, its Pages hosting service has shut down, and the global open-source community, meaning the tools and people you will actually collaborate with, is on GitHub. Learn git and GitHub as the real skill, and treat Gitee as a fast mirror rather than a replacement.

One official tool is worth installing: the GitHub CLI (the gh command), which brings GitHub into the terminal, so cloning a repo, reading issues, opening a pull request, or checking CI status no longer needs a browser. Run gh auth login once after installing, and the point goes beyond saving yourself a few clicks: from then on a coding agent can run gh as you, and most git-plus-GitHub work, from creating repos and pushing code to opening PRs and answering issues, can be delegated to it while you watch the commands go by. Gitee has no official counterpart so far, but the heavy daily operations (clone, push, pull) are plain standard git anyway, so an agent can do those for you just the same; only platform features like issues and PRs need the browser.

Tip

Every tool mentioned on this page, from gh to Oh My Zsh and iTerm2 in Further reading, can be installed by simply telling your coding agent in plain language: "install this for me." Downloading, installing, and configuring are its job. That is exactly why the agent sits on the first page of this roadmap.

docs.title: Learning these with an agent beside you
docs.text:
A coding agent changes the economics of everything on this page. It can write the find pipeline you half-remember, and it reads git's error messages better than most of us ever will. What it cannot do is know whether the command it just proposed is safe to run on data you cannot regenerate. So the skills worth sharpening are the supervisory ones: reading a diff before committing it, pausing at anything that deletes or overwrites, and insisting the agent work inside git so every step stays undoable.

Two habits make the pairing work well. The first is to make the agent your tutor: when it runs a command you do not know, ask it to explain the command flag by flag, or paste it into explainshell. It is a patient teacher, and the explanation arrives attached to your actual problem. The second is to commit more often than feels necessary. With an agent editing at machine speed, the commit is the unit of undo, and small frequent commits are what let you say "that last idea was wrong" without losing the afternoon.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• The Linux Command Line by William Shotts: the book-length version of the shell section, free as a PDF, with a community Chinese translation, 快乐的 Linux 命令行. For when a real problem starts asking for depth.
  • Pro Git: the official reference, free, in Chinese. The first three chapters cover daily life; the rest can wait.
  • 码农高天's 十分钟学会正确的 GitHub 工作流 (Chinese, bilibili): a professional programmer walks through the GitHub workflow open-source authors actually use to maintain code, in ten minutes.
  • Oh My Zsh: a configuration framework for zsh that gets you themes, better completion, and a pile of ready-made plugins; makes the terminal much nicer to live in.
  • iTerm2: the replacement terminal for macOS, much stronger on split panes, search, and shortcuts; on Windows the counterpart is Microsoft's own Windows Terminal.

docs.title: Deep Learning Basics
docs.text: Is deep learning worth sitting down and learning properly? The lab's answer is yes, though probably not the way you'd picture it. What follows: why it's worth the time, what to have in place first, which course to follow, and where it connects onwards.

docs.title: Why it's worth learning
docs.text:
Here's a situation that comes up fast. You open an AI-plus-biology paper, get to the methods, and the authors write that they fine-tuned a pre-trained model. That's the whole explanation. No definition of pre-training, no reason given for fine-tuning, because to them it's common knowledge. Papers in this field are dense with that vocabulary: embedding, loss function, overfitting, attention. Without those words the methods section becomes something to skip, and the methods are usually the part most worth reading.

The second reason is more practical. Most of the time we're not training models from scratch, we're using someone else's: running a structure prediction, scoring a batch of variants. The awkward part is that a model never announces when it's guessing. Hand it a sequence unlike anything in its training data and it still returns a number, formatted exactly like a correct answer. Working out whether that number deserves trust means knowing what data it saw, what objective it optimised, and where its competence runs out. That question comes up far more often in day-to-day work than writing training code does.

One more thing, and this one is reassuring. The foundations here are steadier than you'd expect. Take apart a 2026 frontier model and you still find the same parts people invented between 2015 and 2017, rearranged. What you learn over the next couple of months won't expire.

flowchart TD
    PRE["<b>Before you start</b><br/>Python · command line and a GPU · linear algebra / calculus / probability"]
    PRE --> C1["Preliminaries · linear nets · MLPs · ch. 2–6"]
    C1 --> C2["Convolutional networks · ch. 7–8"]
    C2 --> C3["Recurrent networks · ch. 9–10"]
    C3 --> C4["<b>Attention · Transformers</b> · ch. 11"]
    C4 --> N1["Large language<br/>models & agents"]
    C4 --> N2["Protein models<br/>AlphaFold"]
    C4 --> N3["Genome sequence models<br/>AlphaGenome"]
    C4 --> N4["Cell-state models"]

Figure: the map for this page. Three prerequisites feed into the D2L trunk, which branches into the model families the lab works on.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Not much preparation. Enough Python to write functions and classes and push arrays around with NumPy. Enough command line to ssh into a machine, set up an environment, and get a notebook running. For maths: linear algebra as in knowing what matrix multiplication does, calculus as in derivatives and the chain rule, probability as in distributions and expectations. That's roughly the bar.

A note on GPUs, since it trips people up: none of this requires getting hold of a server first. The models in most of D2L are small enough for a laptop with a discrete GPU, and Google Colab's free tier covers you without one. Cluster time can wait until there's something big to train.

Maths is where people get stuck. The thought "shouldn't I take a semester of linear algebra first" occurs to almost everyone. D2L's preface is explicit that it assumes only basic linear algebra, calculus, probability, and very basic Python, and chapter 2 re-teaches the maths it actually uses. Filling gaps as you go works fine.

Self-check: ready enough?

You can read a chunk of NumPy and say what A @ B computes. You know what taking a derivative means geometrically and you've heard of the chain rule. You can ssh into a machine and get a Python script running. If those three roughly match, this is a fine time to start; if one is a long way off, that one first will make the rest smoother.

docs.title: Following D2L
docs.text:
Dive into Deep Learning (D2L) has essentially no competition as a starting point. It's a book, but every section is a runnable Jupyter notebook, and it's used as a textbook at over 500 universities. The companion video course walks through the material section by section, writing out the PyTorch line by line next to the ideas, though the lectures are in Chinese only.

Worth saying explicitly: even without doing deep learning research, if you're going to use deep learning models then this material is hard to route around.

The chapters don't need equal effort, though stopping too early is a common regret. Chapters 1 to 6 lay the groundwork. Chapters 7 to 11 cover four model families, multilayer perceptrons, convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks, arriving at attention. Chapter 11 is the hinge of the whole book and the ten before it are groundwork for it.

Plenty of people wrap up right there, and there's more worth having. Chapters 12 to 14 cover optimisation and computational performance, which are exactly the problems that show up daily once you train something yourself: setting a learning rate, running out of GPU memory, using more than one card. Chapters 15 and 16 on NLP give the history that led up to LLMs. You see how the BERT generation framed the problem, which is what makes it clear what the GPT series actually changed.

Groundworkch. 1–6 Introduction · Preliminaries · Linear networks · Multilayer perceptrons · Builders' guide Four model familiesch. 7–11 Convolutional networks · Modern CNNs · Recurrent networks · Modern RNNs · Attention and Transformers Training your ownch. 12–14 Optimisation algorithms · Computational performance · Computer vision NLP before LLMsch. 15–16 NLP: pretraining · NLP: applications How to read D2L. The first eleven chapters are the trunk; what follows isn't optional, it just serves a different purpose.

One gap D2L does leave: it never really covers the GPT-1, 2, 3 line. Karpathy fills that in. See the further reading below.

The order for any one section goes like this: watch the video, run the notebook, then change a hyperparameter and watch it break. Raise the learning rate tenfold, halve the layers, switch off the regularisation, then account for what you saw. Step three takes the longest and teaches the most; the first two make it very easy to feel like you've learned something.

The "from scratch" sections are worth the time. They look like busywork, since the very next section redoes the same thing in a few lines of framework code. But they're one of the rare chances to take backpropagation and gradient descent apart by hand, and skipping them tends to leave both as black boxes, along with whatever automatic differentiation was doing on your behalf.

The course comes with four Kaggle competitions, and finishing one properly is worth a lot. The gap between "I ran someone else's notebook" and "I'm looking at data nobody cleaned for me" only closes by crossing it once.

On timing: the trunk is chapters 1 to 11, and at two or three sections a week that's roughly two to three months.

docs.title: Where it goes from here
docs.text:
Those chapters are a junction, and every direction the lab cares about grows out of them.

The Transformer in chapter 11 is the T in GPT, and BERT gets a full section in chapter 15. Read both, add Karpathy's two videos, and large language models stop being a black box. That thread continues at LLMs & Agent Tools.

AlphaFold's core module is a variant of attention that attends over pairs of residues rather than words in a sentence, which leads to Protein Models. Enformer and AlphaGenome are built from convolutions that recognise local sequence patterns plus attention that links a regulatory element to a gene hundreds of kilobases away, so chapters 7 and 8 plus chapter 11, leading to Genome Sequence Models. And Cell-State Models treat a cell as a sentence and its genes as words, carrying the whole language-model playbook across.

Four fields to read about, one box of parts to learn.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
3Blue1Brown's neural network series is four short films that turn neural networks, gradient descent and backpropagation into things you can see. Good before starting D2L, or to come back to when the maths stalls you.

Karpathy's two videos fill the gap D2L leaves. Let's build GPT hand-writes a character-level GPT from nothing in about two hours. Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT runs three and a half hours and goes from pre-training all the way to RLHF; it's the clearest account of the modern LLM training stack I know of.

Deep Learning by Goodfellow et al., the flower book, works better as a reference than a read-through. Look up the chapter when you want to dig into one concept.

docs.title: Genome Sequence Models
docs.text:
AI-generated draft, not yet human-reviewed

An AI agent wrote this whole page. A human has not yet checked or revised it, so treat everything here, the numbers and citations most of all, as provisional until this notice comes down.

A genome sequence model learns the link between a stretch of DNA and what that DNA does. That link runs two ways. Reading it means taking a sequence and predicting a measurement somebody made on it, how open the chromatin is, where a protein binds, how much RNA gets made. Writing it means starting from a functional goal and designing a sequence that meets it, a synthetic enhancer that fires in one cell type and stays silent everywhere else. Most of the field, and most of this page, is about reading; design turns out to be largely the reading model run backwards, and it gets its own section near the end.

Ten years of work stretched the reading models' input window from about a hundred bases to a full megabase. What that mostly bought was better ranking, not better arithmetic: today's models sort candidate variants and regulatory elements sensibly and still understate how much any of them does. What limits them is not how much sequence they see, it is where their training labels came from. This page maps what the model reads, how the field got here, what actually improved, what you can trust it for, how the same machinery designs new DNA, and where the lab fits. It assumes Deep Learning Basics; everything here is convolutions and attention pointed at DNA.

docs.title: What these models actually do
docs.text:
Every model on this page has the same shape. DNA goes in, a measurement comes out. The interesting differences are how much DNA, how finely the output is resolved, and how many kinds of measurement.

DNA is not numbers, so first it becomes numbers. Each base turns into a column of four slots with a 1 in the slot for A, C, G, or T and zeros elsewhere. A 1,000 bp window is a 4 × 1,000 matrix of ones and zeros. That one-hot matrix is the whole answer to "how does a sequence become a tensor."

The output is a stack of tracks. A track is one number per genomic position, produced by one assay in one cell type, so when AlphaGenome reports 5,930 human tracks that number is roughly assays times cell types. Four assays cover most of what these models predict: ATAC-seq and DNase read which stretches of DNA are open and accessible, ChIP-seq reads where a particular protein sits, CAGE reads where transcription starts, and RNA-seq reads how much transcript is present. The assays themselves live in Genomics, and the promoters, enhancers, and transcription factors they measure live in Molecular Biology & Epigenetics. The output is a grid of tracks by bins, and the bin size is the resolution: a 128 bp bin means the model cannot resolve anything finer than 128 bp, which is why AlphaGenome predicting down to single bases is a change in kind, not just a bigger number.

ACGTGGCA ACGT 11111111 4 × L one-hot matrix a filter sliding over one-hot DNA is a position weight matrix, learned model ATAC · cell A ATAC · cell B RNA-seq · cell A 128 bp bins 1 bp one track = one assay × one cell type DNA in, measured tracks out. Sliding a filter over the one-hot matrix is the same operation as scanning a motif, which is where a biologist's existing knowledge meets deep learning.

That last point is the one place your existing knowledge maps exactly onto a neural network. A position weight matrix scanned along a sequence and a convolution filter applied to one-hot DNA are the same operation. The only difference is that a PWM's weights are counted from known binding sites while a filter's weights are learned by gradient descent, which is why the first layer of the earliest model on this page looks like a set of motifs. Scanning alone was never enough, though. Look for a transcription factor's motif genome-wide and almost every hit is a place where nothing happens; whether a site does anything depends on the sequence around it, and that context is what a deep model buys you. This is old news, called the futility theorem back in 2004, and it is the problem the whole field exists to solve.

One more idea makes the rest of the page legible. The number a paper advertises is its input length, but a model does not use all of it. Basenji reads a 131 kb window while any single output position only sees about 32 kb of it, its receptive field, and as we will see even the receptive field overstates what the model actually leans on. Variant effect prediction, finally, is not a separate kind of model. It is predict(ALT) − predict(REF) from a model that never saw a single variant during training, which is exactly why it can score a mutation nobody has ever observed, and exactly why nothing guarantees the difference it reports is causal.

Before reading further, it helps to look at one. ENCODE's SCREEN browser shows measured regulatory elements around any gene you know, and seqnn.org shows predicted and measured brain tracks side by side.

docs.title: How the field got here
docs.text:
1 Mb100 kb10 kb1 kb100 bp 20152018202120242026 DeepSEA Basenji Enformer Borzoi AlphaGenome receptive field ≈ 32 kb, not 131 kb a ~1 kb window already recovers ⅔ of the signal GPN-MSA: 128 bp + a 100-species alignment input window a paper advertises context the model demonstrably uses The input window grew ten-thousandfold in a decade. The context a model demonstrably uses barely moved, and in 2025 a 128 bp model won a variant-scoring task outright. Bigger window is not the axis the field runs on.

The story starts in 2015 with two papers three weeks apart. DeepBind came first and is the clean illustration of the point above, a learnable motif scanner and little more. DeepSEA is the one everything since looks like: one network, 1,000 bp in, 919 chromatin measurements out, and in-silico mutagenesis to turn the trained model into a variant scorer. That last move is what made a sequence model into a human-genetics instrument.

Three years later Basenji changed two things at once, switching from yes-or-no labels to quantitative coverage and jumping from 1 kb to 131 kb with dilated convolutions. Then in 2021 the field split. BPNet went the opposite way on context, reading 1 kb and predicting base-resolution binding profiles, paired with attribution and motif clustering so that its output was mechanism you could take to the bench; it predicted that Nanog binds with a roughly 10.5 bp helical periodicity and that was then confirmed with CRISPR point mutations. Enformer went the other way, swapping dilation for attention and reading 197 kb. Neither BPNet nor its accessibility successor ChromBPNet is an obsolete small model; they are a deliberate choice of the opposite corner. The recent frontier merges the two directions. Borzoi predicts RNA-seq coverage directly, so transcription, splicing, and polyadenylation come out of one head, and AlphaGenome reads a megabase and emits down to single bases across eleven kinds of measurement, leading 25 of 26 variant-effect evaluations in its paper.

Read the timeline together with the figure, though, or it teaches the wrong lesson. GPN-MSA wins genome-wide variant scoring with a small window plus a hundred-vertebrate alignment. ChromBPNet stays competitive on accessibility with about 2 kb. The DREAM challenge winner and a 1.3-million-parameter model that matches Enformer-scale accuracy on reporter data are both tiny. Bigger window is not the axis.

Model (year) Reads Emits What it added DeepBind (2015) ~101 bp one binding score first convolutional net on raw DNA; a learnable motif scanner DeepSEA (2015) 1 kb 919 chromatin labels one network for all of ENCODE, plus in-silico mutagenesis to score variants Basset (2016) 600 bp 164 accessibility labels tuned, open, reusable code; where the field's software culture starts Basenji (2018) 131 kb (uses ~32 kb) 4,229 tracks, 128 bp bins quantitative coverage instead of yes/no; dilation buys range SpliceAI (2019) 15 kb window per-base splice donor/acceptor the one model in routine clinical use BPNet (2021) 1 kb base-resolution TF profiles attribution plus motif clustering; syntax you test at the bench Enformer (2021) 197 kb 5,313 human tracks, 128 bp bins attention in place of dilated convolutions Sei (2022) 4 kb 21,907 profiles → 40 classes more targets, not more context; a vocabulary of regulatory activity ChromBPNet (preprint) 2.1 kb base-resolution ATAC/DNase factors out the enzyme's own cut bias, which footprinting had read as biology Borzoi (2025) 524 kb RNA-seq coverage, 32 bp bins transcription, splicing, polyadenylation from one output AlphaGenome (2026) 1 Mb 5,930 tracks, 11 modalities, to 1 bp range and resolution together; leads 25 of 26 variant evaluations

docs.title: What got better, and what hasn't
docs.text:
Two things improved, and both are worth stating before the criticism. Splicing is the field's one clinical success. Whether a position is a splice donor or acceptor is nearly settled by local sequence, it barely varies across cell types, and it is annotated at effectively every base of the genome, so SpliceAI and Pangolin work well enough that the ClinGen sequence-variant group wrote SpliceAI thresholds into clinical variant classification. The other real gain is direction of effect for expression QTLs: between Borzoi and AlphaGenome the sign-accuracy rose from about 0.75 to 0.80 auROC, and at a strict sign-accuracy cutoff the fraction of GTEx eQTLs recovered went from 19% to 41%. For prioritising a credible set of variants that is a usable jump.

The failure is one problem wearing three coats, and all three are about magnitude. When you knock down a validated enhancer with CRISPRi the median one drops its target gene by about 20%, and Enformer predicts about 4%; for roughly 60% of genes with a validated enhancer, no tested candidate cleared even a 10% predicted effect. Two independent 2026 results find the same compression from other directions: AlphaGenome's quantitative expression effects transfer to mouse but come out compressed roughly a hundredfold against the empirical benchmark while splice-site disruption transfers almost perfectly, and models trained across five mammalian livers predict whether an orthologous region is accessible but not by how much it differs between species.

The sharpest version is what happens when you stop comparing genes and start comparing people. Enformer's headline correlation is computed across genes, where much of the signal is just "is this a housekeeping promoter." Hold the gene fixed and vary the individual and it collapses toward zero. In one brain-cortex benchmark a plain linear model on genotypes significantly predicted 921 genes at a mean correlation of 0.26 while Enformer managed 162 at 0.02, and of the 598 genes where Enformer was significantly correlated with truth, 195 were significantly anti-correlated. Getting the sign backwards is worse than being weak. The honest 2026 refinement is that this is not a blanket failure across individuals but a failure for one modality: AlphaGenome approaches the heritability ceiling for personal chromatin accessibility and stays far below baseline for personal gene expression. Local grammar is largely solved; long-range integration is not.

The diagnostic question to carry into any paper is simple: what is held fixed and what varies. And the rule that follows from all of it: trust the ordering these models give you, not the number.

docs.title: Where the labels come from
docs.text:
Reread that timeline as a story about labels rather than architecture and the whole field snaps into focus. The phases are not "bigger networks," they are new sources of training signal: first bulk assays over the reference genome from ENCODE and Roadmap, then base-resolution assays and designed reporter libraries, then a detour through self-supervision on raw DNA, and now megabase multimodal assays plus counterfactuals manufactured in silico.

The reason this matters is that the genome runs out. de Boer and Taipale put it most sharply: holding out a chromosome does not create independent test data, because homologous sequence straddles the split, and the human genome is simply too short and too undiversified to fit the regulatory code from natural sequence alone. A 2026 follow-up measured that leakage and found memorisation inflates reported accuracy exactly on the sequences most similar to training, worst for the longest-context models.

Designed libraries are the answer that keeps working, because they manufacture the labels the genome cannot supply. The DREAM challenge handed teams 6.7 million random promoters measured in yeast and 19 entries beat the previous state of the art, the winner a small CNN. A 680,000-element reporter library trained a 1.3-million-parameter model to Enformer-level accuracy. Enhancer design works for the same reason, since it only needs correct ranking inside a library it manufactured and then checks the answer at the bench. Causal perturbation data, by contrast, is scarce and mostly from one cell line, which is why the distal-enhancer benchmark everyone quotes rests on a few hundred element-gene pairs in K562.

The self-supervised branch fits the same logic. The idea is to carry the language-model playbook over to DNA, predicting masked or next bases so the model learns sequence structure without labels. It works well in bacteria, whose genomes are 85 to 90% coding and densely constrained, so predicting the next base is nearly a functional objective. Human DNA is about 98% noncoding and mostly unconstrained, and that mismatch shows up in the benchmarks: on counterfactual variant effect a small supervised accessibility model reaches 0.77 to 0.89 auROC against 0.65 to 0.70 for the best fine-tuned language model. Where self-supervision does pay is constraint, coding variants, and indels, and Evo 2 is the only family that can score an insertion or deletion at all. The strongest rebuttal is worth naming rather than burying: pairwise in-silico mutagenesis of a genomic language model's internals recovers RNA structure and transcription-factor binding sites that single-position scoring never saw, so the branch is far from settled.

One quiet detail in AlphaGenome makes the label-supply reading concrete. Its main architectural move is to distil an ensemble into one student using shifted, reverse-complemented, and randomly mutated inputs, and dropping the mutation augmentation measurably hurts variant scoring. That is label manufacturing by another name. So before trusting any number a model gives you, ask who measured its labels and over what sequences.

docs.title: What you can trust it for
docs.text:
Nobody retrains these models. The realistic moves are to fine-tune a small output head, attach a linear probe to frozen embeddings, or just score variants with a released checkpoint, and a frozen-embedding linear probe is almost always the right first experiment. The page above is organised by lineage because that is how the literature is written, but when you are holding a dataset you want the inverse index.

If you want to Reach for Not for this Score a variant near a splice site, clinically SpliceAI or Pangolin, run yourself, at ClinGen thresholds precomputed lookups, or any general sequence-to-function model Score any SNV genome-wide, cheaply GPN-MSA precomputed scores for all ~9 billion human SNVs standing up a multi-billion-parameter model Find motifs and footprints in your own ATAC data ChromBPNet, then tangermeme and TF-MoDISco reading first-layer convolution filters as motifs Prioritise a non-coding GWAS hit AlphaGenome or Borzoi as one line of evidence, using rank and direction treating the predicted number as an effect size Predict accessibility for a cell type you have data for ChromBPNet per pseudobulk; scooby, Decima, or bolero across many states Enformer's bulk ENCODE tracks Design an enhancer for a cell type an oracle trained on your own readout plus directed in-silico evolution a generative model, unless you specifically want diversity Ask what one person's variant does to one gene nothing yet; a linear model on personal genotypes still wins any of the above

Four misconceptions are worth killing directly. "Foundation model" means two unrelated things in this literature, self-supervised pretraining on raw DNA and large multitask supervised models, sometimes inside one review, so say which you mean. Bigger and self-supervised is not automatically better, as the variant benchmark above shows. First-layer convolution filters are not motifs; use context-aware attributions clustered into patterns, DeepSHAP into TF-MoDISco, not filter pictures. And attention weights are not attribution, since they show roughly where a model looked and can be changed without changing the prediction.

docs.title: Designing DNA, not just reading it
docs.text:
Turn a reading model around and it becomes a designer. Instead of scoring a sequence you already have, you fix a goal and search sequence space for a sequence the model says will hit it. The reading model plays oracle, the objective is almost always a contrast (on-target activity minus the strongest off-target, not raw activity), and you synthesise a few hundred candidates, test them at the bench, and feed the measurements back as new training data. De Winter, Konstantakos & Aerts 2025 is the review that lays this loop out; the useful thing to internalise is that the model is the cheap part, and the objective and the assay are where the biology lives.

The workhorse search is directed in silico evolution, greedy point mutation guided by the oracle, and it is a stubbornly strong baseline. Generative priors like GANs and diffusion mostly buy diversity and naturalness rather than higher fitness. The wet-lab record is real. Taskiran et al. 2024 evolved fly enhancers from random sequence that fired in the intended neurons in a live animal. Gosai et al. 2024 designed human regulatory elements that beat natural sequences on cell-type specificity, 94% against 41%. Vaishnav et al. 2022 is the cleanest teaching case: a model trained on tens of millions of random yeast promoters, then run as a fitness landscape, which is what makes it obvious that design and evolution are one computation in two directions. PARM does the same for human promoters with a sub-million-parameter model.

A separate track writes whole genomes rather than single elements. DNA language models like Evo and Evo 2 generate chromosome-scale sequence, and Evo 2 designed chromatin-accessibility patterns that spelled Morse code in living cells, though functional genomes written from scratch stay aspirational and the biosecurity questions are live. For a neuro lab the near-term payoff is cell-type-specific enhancer AAVs, where designed elements are starting to work in the mammalian brain, with the honest caveat that measured open chromatin still beats sequence models at picking which candidates fire.

docs.title: Where the lab fits
docs.text:
The lab's published record is atlas building: single-cell DNA methylation and 3D genome across the mouse and human brain. The move here is to turn those atlases into a training corpus, so the question shifts from "what cell states exist and what is their epigenome" to "what in the sequence encodes them, and which non-coding variants perturb them." That is bolero, a cell-state-conditioned model built on the Borzoi backbone; the paper is in preparation, so cite it as software. See Research Projects.

The magnitude problem from earlier is part of the reason to build it. A bulk track averages over cells where an element is active and cells where it is not, so a compressed prediction may be the correct conditional expectation for a bulk readout, which is an argument for conditioning on cell state rather than a reason to give up. That is what scooby, Decima, and bolero are each doing; see Cell-State Models and Single-Cell Omics. The open lane for a methylation lab is that nothing in the Enformer-to-AlphaGenome line predicts DNA methylation. In a 2026 brain-atlas fine-tune, CpG methylation predicts at 0.94 and non-CG methylation at 0.65. Read those skeptically: mCG is bimodal and mostly follows CpG-island grammar, so 0.94 is the easy number, while mCH is neuron-specific, accumulates after birth, and has no bulk analogue, so 0.65 is both the honest number and the interesting one. See Molecular Biology & Epigenetics.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The awkward truth is that there is no current course covering deep learning for regulatory genomics; the best full lecture series froze in spring 2021, before Borzoi and before AlphaGenome. The best hands-on material now is a library's tutorial folder. A workable ladder: do Deep Learning Basics for the deep learning, take a genomics course for what the assays are, run an AlphaGenome Colab for a same-day first result, work through gReLU's notebooks over a weekend, then bring ChromBPNet and tangermeme to your own data for a real project.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Start with the review that explains mechanics rather than surveying results, Eraslan et al. 2019. For a current single review of sequence-to-expression that adds the training-data lens, read Barbadilla-Martínez et al. 2025; Sokolova et al. 2024 is open access and organises the field by prediction target. The critique thread is short and worth reading in order: Karollus 2023 for the distal-enhancer ablation, the Huang and Sasse pair for the personal-genome collapse, and de Boer and Taipale 2024 for the diagnosis. For where it goes next, Nagai et al. 2026 argue the point this page is built around: predictive accuracy does not automatically become regulatory understanding, and closing that gap needs experiments in the loop. Those papers are the kind we take apart in Journal Club.

docs.title: Writing This Site With Claude Code
docs.text: Every page on this site, including this one, was drafted by Claude Code and revised by a person. That is worth describing not because the site itself is interesting, but because the arrangement copies easily to whatever you are working on.

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text:
The split that works: you decide what is worth saying and whether it is true, and the agent does the building.

A page here starts as a handful of bullet points and some opinions. Claude turns that into a draft, writes the Chinese version alongside the English one, hooks the page into the site navigation, runs the build, and fixes whatever it broke along the way. Then it stops and waits for a person to judge: is this claim actually correct? Does this paragraph sound like a person wrote it?

A useful way to hold it in your head is a fast, tireless collaborator who never finds a chore too boring and sometimes cannot tell what matters. Everything it hands you is a proposal.

docs.title: Getting it into a project
docs.text:
A few habits separate an agent that earns its keep from one that produces plausible mess.

Give it the whole project instead of pasted snippets. It opens files on its own, searches, runs commands, reads the output, and tries again. Passing code back and forth through a chat window throws away most of what it can do.

Write your rules down once. A session begins with no memory of the previous one, so whatever you settled last week gets settled differently this week. This repository keeps a file called CLAUDE.md at its root that the agent reads at the start of every session. It holds the things you would otherwise explain forever: write both languages in the same pass, keep a page readable in one sitting, avoid this particular tone. It runs about a hundred lines, and pound for pound it is the most important file in the project.

Worth spelling out how this "memory" works. The agent remembers nothing on its own; the memory is just that file being read back at the start of every session, CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, AGENTS.md for Kimi Code. So every time you correct it, you can have it write the rule into the file, and it takes effect from the next session on. A step further: workflows you run again and again, like a standard lab analysis, can be packaged as a Skill, a folder of instructions the agent loads only when it is needed. The lab's own Skills live at Routine Lab Support.

Let it check its own work. Given a way to run the build and see the errors, it will fix them before showing you anything. Without one, you become the error message.

docs.title: One case that made the value obvious
docs.text:
We wanted hover definitions on jargon: park the mouse on a term and a small bubble pops up with a one-line explanation, so a reader meeting a word like backpropagation for the first time never has to leave the page. The standard way of doing this turned out not to work on Chinese text at all.

Before, that is where the idea would have died. The problem itself was small: the off-the-shelf plugin does not handle Chinese, so someone had to write the code themselves. The hard part was the cost, half a day away from the real work to learn an interface you would use exactly once, in exchange for a merely nice-to-have feature. Claude Code changed that math: describe the need, and it reads the docs, writes the code, and debugs it, all in one session. Now every page on the site has it.

This is where an agent pays off more than it does on prose. Small improvements that were never worth the interruption become cheap enough to simply do, and a project slowly gets better in ways it otherwise would not have.

docs.title: Where it does not help
docs.text: Taste, framing, and truth: all three ultimately rest on human judgment. The first real page here needed two full revision passes on tone alone, long after every fact in it was correct. The agent will also state something wrong with exactly the confidence it uses to state something right, so reviewing is not optional. That review is most of the work that remains.

docs.text: 本站使用 Markdown 编写，并由 MkDocs 和 Material for MkDocs 构建。 关于如何在本地预览改动，请参阅 README。

docs.title: 大语言模型与 Agent 工具应用
docs.text: 把这一页放在整个学习路线的第一站，是有意安排的。倒不是因为这些工具时髦，而是它们实实在在改变了后面每一样学习的代价。过去遇到一个问题，可能得跟别人的代码耗上一个星期，如今很多时候就是一场对话的事。真正卡脖子的地方，于是从"能不能把代码写出来"挪到了"有没有把问题想明白"。接下来我们会先认识底下的大语言模型，再聊聊这类工具为什么值得花功夫学，几个名字长得很像的东西分别是什么，从哪里上手，以及怎么用它放大自己的能力。

docs.title: 先认识大语言模型
docs.text:
coding agent 的发动机是大语言模型（large language model，LLM），值得先花一点篇幅认识它。它学会的本事说起来只有一样：读了海量的文字之后，给定前面的话，猜下一个词最可能是什么。聊天窗口里那些对答如流，就是这个接龙游戏训练了亿万次之后的样子。记住这一点，后面的很多怪事就好解释了：它不是数据库，说出来的话不保证是真的；它也没有长久的记忆，每次能看到的只有你发给它的那一窗内容，也就是后面会反复提到的上下文窗口。agent 偶尔一本正经地胡说，或者聊久了像换了个人，根子都在这两条上。

用它的人，这几年换了三茬打法。最早是聊天机器人时代，一个问题换一个回答，值得钻研的是怎么把提示词写好，prompt engineering 这个词就是那个年代的产物。后来模型学会了先想再答，推理模型把"一步一步来"从提示词技巧变成了内建的习惯，字斟句酌这件事本身就不那么要紧了。最近的一次变化是把模型放进循环里，给它工具，让它自己读文件、跑命令、看结果、再决定下一步，这就是 agent。人的功夫也跟着挪了地方：从琢磨一句话的措辞，挪到搭一个好用的环境，给清楚的目标、趁手的工具，再加一个能自我检查的抓手。这一页后面讲的"交办而不是口述"，就是这个新打法的日常版本。

想把这些底子一次补齐，可以花半小时过一过 LLM Fundamentals（英文）。它在浏览器里交互着学，不用装任何东西，讲的正是上面这几件事的更底层：system prompt 到底起什么作用，模型为什么是用数字"思考"的，上下文塞太满为什么反而坏事，工具给太多为什么会变慢。概念不多，但每一个都是以后天天要打的交道。

docs.title: 为什么它是第一项基础技能
docs.text:
coding agent 是这样一类程序：你用大白话交代一个目标，它就自己去读文件、跑命令、改代码，一直干到目标达成，或者干不下去为止。再配上命令行和 git，那个原本让人望而生畏的黑色窗口，就成了一个可以商量事情的伙伴。

这件事不管对做实验的还是写程序的，意义都很大，理由有两个。一是 coding agent 不挑地方，不是非得待在代码仓库里才能干活。Anthropic 的文档特意提到，一个装满笔记和手稿的文件夹，对它来说同样好用。这个网站，包括你正在看的这一页，就是这么写出来的，具体过程记在用 Claude Code 写这个网站。二是真正的门槛多半不在写代码，而在理解。Anthropic 分析了大约 40 万次会话后发现，把用得好和用不好的人区分开的，是各自领域的专业功底，而不是编程水平。MIT 在 2026 年 1 月开了一期专门讲 agentic coding 的《Missing Semester》，能为这个话题专门开一门课，本身就说明它确实重要。

对咱们实验室来说，这些工具已经是必须掌握的东西。2026 年年中发布的 Claude Science 自带基因组学、单细胞、结构生物学的工具，还能通过 SSH 操作 HPC 集群，用 sbatch 提交作业，而不是图省事在登录节点上直接跑。Edison Scientific 的 Kosmos 则是另一个方向，定位就是"AI 科学家"：自己读文献、分析数据、提出假设，面向生物医药的研发。用不用这些产品另说，可以预见，这类工具以后会越来越普及。

docs.title: 三样长得很像的东西
docs.text:
刚开始最值得理清的一件事："聊天机器人""coding agent"，再加上 OpenClaw、Hermes 那一类，看起来是三个同类型的产品，其实不是。它们是同一个模型穿了三件厚薄不同的外衣。模型是同一个，而且不管套哪件外衣，它都跑在数据中心里，不在你的电脑上。真正变的是外面那层 harness（外壳），也就是它能调用哪些工具、被允许碰到你手上的哪些东西。

flowchart TB
    C1["<b>网页聊天机器人</b><br/><i>只看得到你粘进去的内容</i>"] --- M
    C2["<b>coding agent</b><br/><i>你的文件、shell 和 git</i>"] --- M
    C3["<b>agent 助手</b><br/><i>你的整台机器和各种账号</i>"] --- M
    M["<b>同一个模型</b> · 跑在数据中心，不在你的笔记本上"]

图：一个模型，三层外壳。从左到右，外壳能碰到的东西越来越多，本事和风险长在同一条轴上。

网页聊天机器人 coding agent agent 助手 举例 claude.ai、ChatGPT Claude Code、Codex CLI、Kimi Code、Z Code OpenClaw、Hermes 外壳跑在哪儿 厂商的服务器上，你只开一个浏览器标签页 你的机器上，终端或编辑器里 你的机器上，在后台运行 能碰到什么 只有你粘进去的东西 你的工作目录、shell 和 git 你整台机器和各种账号 会不会循环 不会，一条消息换一个回复 会，一直调工具到把活干完 会，还能自己发起一轮 能不能撤销 没什么可撤的 能，靠 git 默认不能

这个分类法值得记住，因为表里这几条属性，既决定了本事大小，也决定了闯祸规模。聊天机器人删不掉你的文件，因为它根本看不见；coding agent 看得见也动得了，所以才一定要在 git 里用它，这样它的每一处改动都是一段 diff，你能逐行读，也能一键退回。OpenClaw、Hermes 这类 agent 助手走得更远，把模型接进邮件、聊天和日历，不用等你发话就能自己动手。方向确实是朝那边走的，不过这类工具眼下还不成熟，可以慢慢了解，用的时候多留个心眼。

想把底下的概念弄清楚，有两篇短文最省事：Simon Willison 给 agent 下的一句话定义（agent 就是让大模型在循环里调用工具去达成目标），以及 Anthropic 的 Building Effective Agents。中文材料里，一口气拆穿 Skill/MCP/RAG/Agent 底层逻辑这个视频用十五分钟讲了同样的事，而且直击要害：这些词人人挂在嘴边，却没几个人真的给它们下过定义。

docs.title: 从哪里上手
docs.text:
上手很简单，打开终端装一个就能开始。Anthropic 的安装指南会带你走一遍流程，快速上手从安装讲到第一次真正的改动；从没碰过命令行的话，还有一份专门的终端指南。

Claude Code 也不是唯一的选择，同类工具还有 Kimi Code、智谱的 Z Code 等，思路和用法大同小异。Kimi Code 在终端里一行命令就能装好（curl -fsSL https://code.kimi.com/kimi-code/install.sh | bash），装完输入 kimi 就能开始。这一页讲的概念和习惯在哪家工具上都通用，先挑一个顺手的用熟，比纠结选哪个更重要。

不过终端迟早值得认真学，git 和集群都住在终端里，"看着 agent 干活"和"自己能检查它干得对不对"之间，隔的也就是这一层。如果要深入学习终端，Linux、Git 与 GitHub 基础那一页讲 shell 和版本控制，Python 基础讲实验室大部分分析在用的语言。

再说句实在话：好用的 coding agent 都是收费的，但这个钱值得花，实验室全力支持大家在这上面的开销。

docs.title: 怎么跟它好好说话
docs.text:
从聊天机器人转过来的人，大多带着同一个习惯：字斟句酌写一条又长又细的指令，然后听天由命。对 agent 来说，这套思路基本是反的。有两个习惯，比任何措辞技巧都管用。

第一个是把活交办出去，而不是一句句口述。把整个项目和目标一起交给它，让它自己去翻文件、搜东西、动手试，而不是把几段代码粘进对话框，再描述你想怎么处理它们。它本来就是在"终端里四处翻看"这种用法上练出来的，放手让它自己看，比你逐句讲给它听，能做成的事多得多。

第二个是给它一个能自我检查的抓手。agent 觉得活干完了就会停，所以只要留一个能跑的测试、一个要过的构建，它就会一直干到检查通过，而不是反过来等你当那个报错信息。就这一个习惯换来的可靠性，胜过任何遣词造句的窍门。

具体细节，看三份材料就够了。Anthropic 的提示最佳实践是最权威的参考，篇幅比你想象的短。Claude Code 最佳实践那篇有前后对照的例子，还有一个很值得学的招：开工之前，先让 agent 就这个任务反过来采访你，把需求写成文档再动手。想学思路而不是句式的话，Anthropic Academy 有门免费的 AI Fluency 课，整门课讲的就是怎么交办、怎么判断，而不是提示词配方。至于任何号称传授"魔法咒语清单"的材料，不管哪种语言写的，都可以直接跳过，在现在的模型上，那套东西基本已经过时了。

docs.title: 你会反复听到的几个词
docs.text:
有一小撮词会一遍遍出现。入门阶段都不用深究，想先把它们全弄懂再动手，反而容易原地踏步。下面每个词给一句话的解释，再附上"哪天它开始挡路了该去哪儿看"的出处。

概念 是什么 从这里开始 模型与 effort 跑哪个模型，以及它回答之前愿意下多大功夫。它明明理解了任务还是做错，就换个更大的模型；要是步骤马虎漏了，就把 effort 调高。 选模型与 effort 上下文窗口 模型一次能看到的全部内容。会话一长就会塞满，塞满之后回答质量会掉。 Explore the context window Skills 一个教 agent 走某套流程的文件夹，只在用得上的时候才加载。现在已经是好几个工具都认的通用标准。 agentskills.io MCP 把 agent 接到数据库这类外部系统的一个通用接口。现在由 Linux 基金会托管，不再归 Anthropic。 modelcontextprotocol.io 子 agent 在自己独立的上下文里干杂活的帮手，只把摘要交回来，主线这边保持干净。 Claude Code 文档

实验室自己也维护了一套 Skills，打包成一个 Claude Code 插件，见常规实验室支持。等你上手以后，工具就是从那儿开始，从"通用"变成"懂我们的数据"。

docs.title: 系统地学一遍
docs.text:
想跟着课程系统地学一遍的话，推荐 DeepLearning.AI 与 Anthropic 合办的短课 Claude Code: A Highly Agentic Coding Assistant，由 Anthropic 的技术教育负责人主讲，从 CLAUDE.md、上下文管理一路讲到子 agent、hooks 和 MCP，中间穿插三个完整的项目练习，最好已经摸过一点 Python 和 git。B 站上有完整视频。

课里用的是 Claude Code，但学完不用怕被绑在这一家工具上：上下文管理、子 agent、hooks、MCP 这些概念在各家 coding agent 上是通用的，换成 Kimi Code、Z Code 照样用得上。

docs.title: 延伸阅读
docs.text:
• Building Effective Agents："把 agent 的架子搭简单点"这个主张最好的短论，等上面那套词不再是一团雾之后，读它正合适。
  • learn.shareai.run：原生中文的课，讲透 Claude Code 为什么会这样做事。内容比较深，近乎从源码层面拆解 Claude，适合想往原理里钻的时候看。
  • MIT 《Missing Semester》 2026 年 1 月那一期：专门讲 agentic coding，顺着它把工具链系统过一遍很合适。
  • 各家官方文档是日常最常回去查的地方：Claude Code 文档、Kimi Code 文档、Z Code 文档。

docs.title: Linux 和 Git、GitHub 基础
docs.text: 命令行、Git 和 GitHub 是实验室日常工作流的基础：敲命令驱动服务器上的计算，Git 记录每一次重要文件的改动，GitHub 把这份历史分享出去，变成协作。磨刀不误砍柴工，这几样加上 Python，就是我们做一切计算和分析的刀；Python 内容多，放在下一页 Python 基础 里单独讲。这三样恰好也是 coding agent 最依赖的技能，所以学的重点不再是背命令，而是读懂 agent 干了什么，判断它做的事情是否必要。这一页挑出值得学的基础，配几份入门材料，再给几个能检查自己是不是真会了的地方。

docs.title: 为什么终端还值得认真学
docs.text:
理由都很实际。第一，实验室的计算大多不在你的笔记本上：测序数据太大，比对太慢，活都在服务器和集群上跑，那些机器没有桌面也没有鼠标，用 SSH 登录进去，迎接你的就是一个 shell。第二，绝大多数生信工具根本没有图形界面，想用就得敲命令。第三，敲命令本身就是效率的来源：shell 的思路是把只干一件事的小工具用管道串起来，上一个的输出直接喂给下一个，所以"从一堆 FASTQ 文件里数出每条序列出现的次数、排出前十"这种事，在编辑器里没法做，在 shell 里只是把 grep、sort、uniq 串起来的一行命令。敲过的命令存进脚本，也随时可以重跑，可以原样交给别人。

有两个词经常被人混着用，值得先分清楚：终端是你屏幕上那个窗口，shell 是窗口里负责读你的命令、把它跑起来的程序，常见的是 bash 和 zsh。Linux 则是那些服务器几乎都在用的操作系统，所以对我们来说，"学 Linux"和"学命令行"基本是同一件事。

coding agent 的出现让这些事更重要了，而不是更不重要。agent 正是在终端和文本流的世界里训练出来的，命令行是它最强的主场，上一页已经讲过。真正变得稀缺的能力，从"会敲命令"挪到了"读得懂命令"：在放 rm -rf 跑之前知道它会干什么，看得出 agent 写的一行命令回答的是你问的问题，还是另一个问题。

docs.title: 学 shell 的路径
docs.text:
按我们的经验，顺序是先文件，再文本流，最后远程机器。先学怎么走动和看东西：ls、cd、cat、less、mkdir、cp、mv、rm。然后学会用流的方式思考：管道、重定向、grep、wc，以及在你发现自己同一条命令敲了十遍的时候，学一个循环。再然后才是用 ssh 和 scp 上远程机器，到这一步，集群就不再是个抽象概念了。到这儿为止，应付实验室的日常工作其实已经够了；写脚本之类的事，也就是把一串命令存进一个文件、让 shell 照着从头跑到尾，等你重复敲烦了，自然会觉得需要它。

第一门课我们推荐 Data Carpentry 的 shell-genomics：它教的正是上面这套东西，但放在一个基因组学项目里，用的例子全是大肠杆菌变异检测数据里的真 FASTQ 文件，每条命令都对着一个真问题。不过它预设了工作坊的云端环境，要自己折腾一番才能跟上；想零准备、在自己笔记本上直接开始的话，可以选 Software Carpentry 的 shell-novice，下载一份小数据，一个下午过完。不管跟哪门课，旁边都建议开着阮一峰的《Bash 脚本教程》当中文参考书，随查随用。偏好听课胜过动手跟练的话，MIT《Missing Semester》的 Shell 课有社区翻译的中文版，把同样的内容浓缩成几讲，信息密度高，适合跟完一门课之后回头快速串一遍。要读的就这些，深度等真问题来敲门的时候再说。

学没学会，得有地方检查，这三个免费网站按真实程度由低到高给你把关。Linux Survival 每个短模块结尾有个小测，让你敲出正确的命令，适合十分钟的回忆式自测。cmdchallenge 在浏览器终端里一题考一条命令，答案自动判对错，不用注册。OverTheWire 的 Bandit 是压轴：通过 SSH 登上一台真实的服务器，每一关的密码就是下一关的门票，能往前走本身就是证明。前 15 关正好覆盖这一页讲的基础，不看答案把它们过完，"命令行我会了"这句话就有了一个很硬的标准。

还有一个建议，属于好玩的那类。Hacknet 是一个剧情驱动的黑客游戏，Steam 上很便宜，自带官方简体中文，整个游戏就是对着终端敲命令来玩。它日常用的命令都是真的 Unix 命令，ls、cd、cat、rm、ps、kill，而且剧情本身就是教程，把命令一个一个介绍给你。不过里面的黑客环节是简化过的想象，也没有管道和权限那一套，所以它教的是对终端的熟悉感，不是真的安全技术。单说消除对黑色窗口的恐惧，它的效果好得出奇。

docs.title: Git，代码的实验记录本
docs.text:
git 是一个版本控制系统：它把一个文件夹的历史记成一串 commit，每个 commit 是一份快照，附带一句话说明这次改动为什么存在。项目一旦进了 git，"我把东西改坏了，还不知道是哪一步坏的"就不再可怕，因为任何早先的状态都只要一条命令就能回去。branch（分支）让你把一个新想法放进平行的草稿里试，不碰正在用的版本。而跟 coding agent 协作时，git 是让"交办"变得安全的那块地基：agent 的每一处改动都是一个 diff，你可以逐行读，也可以一键退回。上一页坚持要在 git 里跑 agent，原因就在这里。

值得尽早建立的直觉是：你的代码同时住在四个地方。

flowchart LR
    A["<b>Working folder</b><br/><i>the files you edit</i>"] -- "git add" --> B["<b>Staging area</b><br/><i>the next snapshot being assembled</i>"]
    B -- "git commit" --> C["<b>Local repository</b><br/><i>the full history on your machine</i>"]
    C -- "git push" --> D["<b>Remote</b><br/><i>GitHub or Gitee</i>"]
    D -- "git pull" --> C

图：一次改动依次经过的四个地方。用 git 时的大多数困惑，其实都是搞混了自己正在看哪一个。

学习资料，两份就够覆盖基础。廖雪峰的 Git 教程是中文世界标准的入门读物：零背景假设，一条命令一条命令地讲，配截图，而且刻意只讲你真正用得上的那些命令。然后是 Learn Git Branching，一个交互式沙盘，提交历史画成动画，有完整中文界面。分支和合并恰恰是教程帮不上忙、只能靠直觉的地方，养这个直觉没有比它更快的。

Learn Git Branching 同时就是自查工具：每一关给一棵目标提交树，你的树和目标对上才算过关，所以把主线和远程两个部分通关，本身就说明技能真的长在手上了。想再证明它在真实的 git 上也作数，gitexercises.fracz.com 会在你本地克隆的仓库里出题，每次跑 git verify 都由服务器判分。这两个工具给你放行，比把教程重读几遍更能说明问题。

docs.title: GitHub，以及 Gitee
docs.text:
GitHub 是上面那张图里 remote 通常所在的地方，但它真正重要的理由在别处：开放科学发生在那里。这份路线里提到的几乎每一个工具和数据集，都以公开仓库的形式住在 GitHub 上，代码、issue、讨论都挂在旁边。会读一个工具的仓库，它的 README、它的 issue 区，本身就是一项研究技能。要学的概念有两个：pull request，把"请把我的改动合并进你的历史"打包成一份可以评审的提案；以及 issue，一条围绕某个 bug 或计划的、可持续跟踪的讨论串。

读到这里，如果还没有账号，先去 GitHub 和 Gitee 各注册一个，下面的练习都要在自己的账号里做。最快的入口是 GitHub 官方的 Hello World，十分钟的练习，全程在浏览器里做，不用装任何东西，把仓库、分支、commit、pull request 走一遍。然后让 GitHub Skills 来检查你：它的免费课程直接在你自己的账号里进行，机器人会自动评审你每一步的操作，所以完成 Introduction to GitHub 这门课，本身就是"这套流程我能走下来"的证明。

从国内访问 GitHub 能用，但常常很慢，开源中国运营的 Gitee 是值得知道的国内方案。它说的是完全一样的 git 语言，clone、push、分支、pull request 都和你预期的一样工作，而且一个仓库可以同时挂两个 remote：同一份代码，一份推给 GitHub 面向世界，一份推给 Gitee 方便国内快速访问。有几句实话也要讲：在 Gitee 上把仓库设为公开需要通过内容审核，它的 Pages 静态托管服务已经下线，而全球的开源社区，也就是你真正会打交道的那批工具和同行，都在 GitHub 上。所以把 git 和 GitHub 当作要学的真本事，把 Gitee 当作一面访问更快的镜子，而不是替代品。

还有一个官方工具值得装：GitHub CLI（命令是 gh），它把 GitHub 的操作搬进了终端，克隆仓库、看 issue、开 pull request、查 CI 状态都不用再开浏览器。装好之后跑一次 gh auth login 登录，这件事的意义不止于你自己少点几下鼠标：登录是一次性的，从那以后 coding agent 就能以你的身份跑 gh，绝大多数 git 加 GitHub 的工作，从建仓库、推代码到开 PR、回 issue，都可以交给它做，你在旁边看它跑命令就行。Gitee 这边目前没有官方的对应工具，好消息是日常最重的操作（clone、push、pull）用的本来就是标准 git，agent 一样能替你做，只有 issue、PR 这类平台功能需要回到浏览器。

小提示

这一页提到的工具，不管是 gh 还是延伸阅读里的 Oh My Zsh、iTerm2，安装都可以直接用自然语言交代给 coding agent，一句"帮我装好这个"，下载、安装、配置它都会搞定。这正是我们把 agent 放在整个路线第一页的原因。

docs.title: 有 agent 陪在旁边，这些怎么学
docs.text:
coding agent 改变了这一页所有内容的投入产出比。你记不太全的 find 管道，它能随手写出来；git 的报错信息，它比我们大多数人都读得熟。它做不到的是判断：它刚提议的这条命令，跑在你无法再生的数据上安不安全。所以值得持续打磨的是那些监督性的技能：提交之前读懂 diff，遇到删除或覆盖的操作先停一拍，以及坚持让 agent 在 git 里干活，让每一步都可以撤销。

有两个习惯能让这种配合运转良好。一是把 agent 当成家教：它跑了你没见过的命令，就让它一个参数一个参数地讲给你听，或者把命令粘进 explainshell。它是个耐心的老师，而且讲解正好落在你眼前的真问题上。二是 commit 得比直觉需要的更勤。agent 以机器的速度改东西，commit 就是撤销的最小单位，小而频繁的 commit，才能让你说出"刚才那个思路不对"的时候，不用赔上一整个下午。

docs.title: 延伸阅读
docs.text:
• William Shotts 的 The Linux Command Line：shell 那部分的书本长度版本，PDF 免费，有社区翻译的中文版《快乐的 Linux 命令行》。等真问题开始要求深度的时候读它。
  • Pro Git：官方参考书，免费，中文。前三章覆盖日常，剩下的可以先放着。
  • 码农高天的《十分钟学会正确的 GitHub 工作流》（B 站）：一个专业程序员讲开源作者们实际使用的工作流，怎么一步步把代码维护起来。
  • Oh My Zsh：zsh 的配置框架，装上就有了好看的主题、更强的补全和一大把现成插件，终端会好用很多。
  • iTerm2：macOS 上替代自带终端的选择，分屏、搜索、快捷键都强得多；Windows 上对应的是微软自家的 Windows Terminal。

docs.title: 深度学习基础
docs.text: 深度学习要不要专门花时间学一遍？这一页是实验室的建议：值得，不过学法可能和想象中不太一样。下面写的是为什么值得、开始之前要会点什么、跟着哪门课走，以及学完之后能接到哪里去。

docs.title: 为什么值得学
docs.text:
先说一个很快就会遇到的场景。打开一篇 AI 加生物的论文，翻到方法部分，作者写"我们在预训练模型上做了微调"，然后就没有然后了。他不解释什么叫预训练，也不解释为什么要微调，因为在他眼里这属于常识。这类词在这个领域的论文里密度很高：嵌入、损失函数、过拟合、注意力机制。不认识它们，方法部分基本只能跳过去，而方法部分往往是一篇论文里最值得读的地方。

第二个理由更实际一些。多数时候我们不会自己从头训练模型，而是用别人训好的：跑一次结构预测，给一批变异打个分。麻烦在于，模型不会告诉你它什么时候在瞎猜。碰到没见过的序列，它照样吐出一个分数，格式和真实结果一模一样。要判断这个分数值不值得信，得知道它拿什么数据训的、优化的是什么目标、什么情况超出了它的能力范围。这件事在日常工作里出现的频率，比自己写训练代码高得多。

还有一点：这个领域的地基比想象中稳定。2026 年最前沿的那些模型，拆开看还是 2015 到 2017 年那几样零件的重新组合。现在花两三个月学的东西，两年后不会作废。

flowchart TD
    PRE["<b>开始之前</b><br/>Python · 命令行与一块 GPU · 线性代数 / 微积分 / 概率"]
    PRE --> C1["预备知识 · 线性网络 · 多层感知机 · 第 2–5 章"]
    C1 --> C2["卷积神经网络 · 第 6–7 章"]
    C2 --> C3["循环神经网络 · 第 8–9 章"]
    C3 --> C4["<b>注意力机制 · Transformer</b> · 第 10 章"]
    C4 --> N1["大语言模型<br/>与 Agent"]
    C4 --> N2["蛋白质模型<br/>AlphaFold"]
    C4 --> N3["基因组序列模型<br/>AlphaGenome"]
    C4 --> N4["细胞状态模型"]

图：这一页的地图。三样前置知识汇入 D2L 的主干，主干再分叉成实验室几个具体的模型方向。

docs.title: 开始之前
docs.text:
准备工作不多。Python 会写函数和类、用 NumPy 处理过数组就够；命令行能 ssh 到一台机器上，装好环境，把 notebook 跑起来。数学方面，线性代数知道矩阵乘法在干什么，微积分知道导数和链式法则，概率知道分布和期望，差不多就可以了。

顺带说一句 GPU：学这个不一定要先搞到一台服务器。D2L 前大半本书的模型都很小，一台带独立显卡的笔记本跑得动，手头没有显卡的话 Colab 的免费额度也够折腾。等真要训大模型了再去申请集群也来得及。

数学是最容易让人卡住的一环。"是不是得先补一学期线代"这个念头大概每个人都有过，实际上 D2L 的前言写得很明白：它只假设读者了解基础的线性代数、微积分、概率和很基础的 Python 编程，而且第 2 章会把后面真正用到的数学重新讲一遍。缺的部分边学边补就行。

自测：够不够？

能读懂一段 NumPy 代码，知道 A @ B 在算什么；知道求导在几何上是什么意思，听说过链式法则；能 ssh 到一台机器上把 Python 脚本跑起来。这三条大致对得上就可以开始了，某一条差得比较远的话，先补那一条会顺一些。

docs.title: 跟着 D2L 走
docs.text:
《动手学深度学习》（简称 D2L）在中文世界里几乎没有对手。它是一本书，但每一节都是能直接跑的 Jupyter notebook；配套的 B 站视频由李沐一节一节讲下来，讲清模型思想的同时把 PyTorch 实现一行行写出来。中英文版被全球五百多所大学拿去当教材。

值得说明的是，就算不做深度学习研究、只是需要用到深度学习模型，这门课里的内容基本也是绕不开的。

资源 用途 中文书 主教材，每节都可运行 B 站视频 李沐逐节讲解，共八十余讲 课程主页 每讲的 PDF 讲义和 notebook GitHub 源码，本地跑代码从这里克隆 官方讨论区 每一节都有对应的提问帖 习题解答 Datawhale 社区整理，卡住时对答案 英文书 章节更多，多出强化学习、高斯过程、超参数优化等

十六章不必平均用力，也不太建议停得太早。第 1 到 5 章打底；第 6 到 10 章讲四类模型，多层感知机、卷积神经网络、循环神经网络，最后落到注意力机制。第 10 章是全书的枢纽，前面九章都在为它铺路。

不少人读到第 10 章就收工了，其实后面还有值得读的部分。第 11 到 13 章讲优化算法和计算性能，这些正是真要自己训一个模型时每天都会撞上的问题：学习率怎么调，显存不够怎么办，多卡怎么用。第 14、15 章的自然语言处理给了 LLM 出现之前的历史背景，能看到 BERT 那一代人怎么想问题，也就明白了 GPT 系列究竟改了什么。

打底第 1–5 章 引言 · 预备知识 · 线性神经网络 · 多层感知机 · 深度学习计算 四类模型第 6–10 章 卷积神经网络 · 现代卷积网络 · 循环神经网络 · 现代循环网络 · 注意力机制与 Transformer 自己训模型第 11–13 章 优化算法 · 计算性能 · 计算机视觉 LLM 之前的 NLP第 14–15 章 自然语言处理：预训练 · 自然语言处理：应用 D2L 的读法。前十章是主干，第 11 章之后不是可选内容，只是各自服务于不同目的。

有一块 D2L 确实没覆盖：GPT-1、2、3 这条线它没细讲。这部分可以看 Karpathy，见文末的延伸阅读。

学一节的顺序大致是：看视频，把 notebook 跑一遍，然后改一个超参数看它怎么坏掉。学习率调大十倍，层数砍一半，正则项关掉，再解释一下看到的现象。第三步最花时间也最有用，前两步很容易产生"已经学会了"的错觉。

"从零开始实现"那些小节值得花时间。它们看着像重复劳动，因为紧接着就有一节用几行框架代码做同样的事。但那是少有的一次亲手把反向传播和梯度下降拆开看的机会，跳过去的话它们大概会一直是个黑箱，也不太会知道自动微分到底替我们做了什么。

课程配了四场 Kaggle 竞赛，挑一场认真做完收获会大很多。从"跑通了别人的 notebook"到"面对一份没人整理过的数据"，这中间的落差只能靠亲自做一次补上。

时间上，主干第 1 到 10 章，每周两三节的话大概两三个月。

docs.title: 学完之后往哪儿走
docs.text:
这十章是个分叉口，实验室关心的几个方向都从这里长出来。

第 10 章的 Transformer 就是 GPT 里的那个 T，BERT 在第 14 章有完整一节。把这两处读完，再补上 Karpathy 的两个视频，大语言模型基本就不是黑箱了。这条线接 大语言模型与 Agent 工具应用。

AlphaFold 的核心模块是注意力的一个变体，只不过它注意的不是句子里的词，而是序列上的残基对，往下走是 蛋白质模型。Enformer、AlphaGenome 这一类的骨架则是卷积负责认出局部序列模式、注意力负责把几十万碱基外的调控元件和基因连起来，正好是第 6、7 章加第 10 章，往下走是 基因组序列模型。至于 细胞状态模型，思路是把一个细胞当成一个句子、把基因当成词，于是整套语言模型的做法就搬了过来。

读起来是四个领域，拆开是同一个零件箱。

docs.title: 延伸阅读
docs.text:
3Blue1Brown 神经网络系列（中文频道，四集短片）把神经网络、梯度下降、反向传播画成了看得见的东西。适合在啃 D2L 之前先看一遍，或者被数学卡住的时候回来看。

Karpathy 的两个视频补上 D2L 缺的那块，都是英文。Let's build GPT 从零手写一个字符级 GPT，两小时；Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT 三个半小时，从预训练一路讲到 RLHF，是目前把现代 LLM 训练全流程讲清楚的最好材料。

花书《深度学习》有中文翻译，也有英文原版。这本更适合当工具书查，想深挖某个概念时翻对应那一章，通读的性价比不高。

docs.title: 基因组序列模型
docs.text:
AI 生成草稿，尚未人工审阅

这一整页由 AI agent 生成，还没有经过人工核对或修改。在本提示撤下之前，请把页面里的所有内容，尤其是数字和引用，都当作暂定。

基因组序列模型学的是一段 DNA 和这段 DNA 的功能之间的联系。这个联系可以往两个方向走。"读"是拿一段序列，预测别人在它上面测出来的某个量：染色质有多开放、某个蛋白落在哪里、转录出多少 RNA。"写"则是从一个功能目标出发，设计一段能达成它的序列，比如一个只在某一种细胞类型里活跃、在别处都沉默的合成增强子。这个领域的大部分、也是这一页的大部分，讲的是读；而设计基本上就是把读的模型反过来跑，它有单独的一节放在靠后的位置。

十年下来，读的这些模型的输入窗口从大约一百个碱基拉长到了整整一兆碱基。而这主要换来的是更好的排序，而不是更准的数值：今天的模型能把候选变异和调控元件排出合理的次序，却仍然低估它们各自的作用有多大。限制它们的，不是能看多长的序列，而是训练标签从哪儿来。这一页梳理模型读入什么、这个领域是怎么走到今天的、到底什么变好了、你能信任它做什么、同一套机器又怎么设计出新的 DNA，以及实验室的位置在哪里。它假设你读过 深度学习基础：这里的一切，无非是把卷积和注意力机制对准了 DNA。

docs.title: 这些模型到底在做什么
docs.text:
这一页上的每个模型形状都一样。DNA 进去，一个测量值出来。有意思的差别在于：喂多长的 DNA、输出分辨到多细、以及能预测多少种测量。

DNA 不是数字，所以第一步是把它变成数字。每个碱基变成四个格子，A、C、G、T 对应的那个格子填 1，其余填 0。一段 1,000 bp 的窗口就成了一个 4 × 1,000 的 0-1 矩阵。这个独热矩阵，就是"序列如何变成张量"的全部答案。

输出是一叠 track。一条信号轨迹是每个基因组位置一个数值，来自某一种实验在某一种细胞类型上的测量，所以当 AlphaGenome 报告 5,930 条人类 track 时，这个数字大致就是实验种类乘以细胞类型数。四种实验覆盖了这些模型要预测的大部分内容：ATAC-seq 和 DNase 读取哪些 DNA 片段开放、可及，ChIP-seq 读取某个特定蛋白落在哪里，CAGE 读取转录从哪里起始，RNA-seq 读取有多少转录本。实验本身见 基因组学，它们测量的启动子、增强子和转录因子见 分子与表观遗传学。输出是一个 track 乘分箱的网格，分箱大小就是分辨率：128 bp 的分箱意味着模型分辨不出比 128 bp 更细的东西，这也是为什么 AlphaGenome 能预测到单碱基是一个实打实的变化，而不只是一个更大的数字。

ACGTGGCA ACGT 11111111 4 × L 独热矩阵 滤波器在独热 DNA 上滑动 其实就是一个学出来的位置权重矩阵 模型 ATAC · 细胞 A ATAC · 细胞 B RNA-seq · 细胞 A 128 bp 分箱 1 bp 一条 track = 一种实验 × 一种细胞类型 DNA 进，测出来的 track 出。让滤波器在独热矩阵上滑动，和扫描一个基序是同一个操作，这正是生物学家已有的知识和深度学习接上头的地方。

最后这一点，是你已有的知识和神经网络严丝合缝对上的唯一一处。一个位置权重矩阵沿序列扫描，和一个卷积滤波器作用在独热 DNA 上，是同一个操作。差别只在于 PWM 的权重是从已知结合位点数出来的，而滤波器的权重是靠梯度下降学出来的，这也是为什么这一页上最早那个模型的第一层看起来就像一组基序。但光靠扫描从来都不够。在全基因组里找某个转录因子的基序，几乎每一个命中的位置都什么也不发生；一个位点到底管不管用，取决于它周围的序列，而这份上下文正是深度模型给你买来的东西。这不是新闻，2004 年就被叫做"徒劳定理"，它正是整个领域存在要去解决的那个问题。

还有一个概念能让这一页后面的内容读起来通顺。论文标称的是它的输入长度，但模型并不会用满这段长度。Basenji 读入一个 131 kb 的窗口，而任何单个输出位置其实只看得到其中约 32 kb，这就是它的感受野，而我们后面会看到，连感受野都高估了模型真正倚重的部分。至于变异效应预测，它根本不是另一类模型，而是 predict(ALT) − predict(REF)，出自一个训练时从没见过任何变异的模型，这正是它为什么能给一个谁都没观测过的突变打分，也正是为什么它报出来的这个差值没有任何东西担保是因果的。

在往下读之前，先去看一个真实的例子会很有帮助。ENCODE 的 SCREEN 浏览器能展示任意一个你熟悉的基因周围实测到的调控元件，而 seqnn.org 则把预测的和实测的大脑 track 并排放在一起。

docs.title: 这个领域是怎么走到今天的
docs.text:
1 Mb100 kb10 kb1 kb100 bp 20152018202120242026 DeepSEA Basenji Enformer Borzoi AlphaGenome 感受野 ≈ 32 kb，而非 131 kb 约 1 kb 的窗口就已恢复 ⅔ 的信号 GPN-MSA：128 bp + 一份百物种比对 论文标称的输入窗口 模型真正用到的上下文 十年间输入窗口涨了一万倍。而模型真正用得到的上下文几乎没动，2025 年甚至有一个 128 bp 的模型在变异打分上完胜。窗口更大，不是这个领域真正在跑的那根轴。

故事从 2015 年相隔三周的两篇论文开始。DeepBind 更早，也是上面那个道理的干净示范，一个能学习的基序扫描器，仅此而已。DeepSEA 则是此后一切都长得像它的那一篇：一个网络，1,000 bp 进，919 个染色质测量出，再用计算机模拟突变把训练好的模型变成一个变异打分器。正是最后这一步，让序列模型成了一件人类遗传学的仪器。

三年后，Basenji 一口气改了两件事，从"有或无"的标签换成定量的覆盖信号，又用扩张卷积把窗口从 1 kb 跳到 131 kb。到了 2021 年，领域分了岔。BPNet 在上下文上走了相反方向，只读 1 kb，却预测单碱基分辨率的结合谱，再配上归因和基序聚类，于是它的输出是可以拿去实验台验证的机理；它预测 Nanog 以大约 10.5 bp 的螺旋周期性结合，随后就用 CRISPR 点突变得到了证实。Enformer 走了另一条路，用注意力机制替换扩张卷积，读入 197 kb。BPNet 和它的可及性后继者 ChromBPNet 都不是过时的小模型，而是刻意选了相反的那个角落。近来的前沿把两个方向合到了一起。Borzoi 直接预测 RNA-seq 覆盖信号，于是转录、剪接、多聚腺苷酸化从一个输出头一起出来，而 AlphaGenome 读入一兆碱基、输出细到单碱基、横跨十一种测量，在其论文里领先 26 项变异效应评测中的 25 项。

不过读这条时间线时得和图一起读，否则它教给你的是错的教训。GPN-MSA 用一个小窗口加一份百物种比对，就赢下了全基因组的变异打分。ChromBPNet 靠约 2 kb 在可及性上依然有竞争力。DREAM 挑战赛的冠军，和一个在报告基因数据上追平 Enformer 级精度的 130 万参数模型，都小得很。窗口更大，不是那根轴。
